abstract: An NBER working paper by Nicholas Bloom, Gideon Moore, Lisa K. Simon and Caelan Wilkie-Rogers showing that public professional profile data, the substrate for a large and growing share of labor market research, is not a stable historical record. Using monthly vintages of Revelio Labs data from 2020 to 2026, the authors document that workers routinely go back and rewrite the titles and descriptions of jobs they have already left. The paper is a measurement contribution: it establishes that a time series reconstructed from profile data can change after the fact without any underlying employment having changed, and that the direction of those revisions is systematically related to labor market transitions and to prevailing vocabulary.
keyFindings: "19.7 percent of established U.S. LinkedIn users retroactively edit the title or description of a job they have already left," measured across monthly vintages from 2020 to 2026.
Profile records "are not fixed historical snapshots, but mutable accounts that workers revise over time."

Retroactive editing is not random with respect to labor market state: users who edit early "are much more likely to change employers as compared to later-editing users," so revisions cluster around job transitions.
"This mutability can bias historical measures of skills" reconstructed from profile text.

Edit content tracks prevailing vocabulary rather than underlying task change: sharp increases in AI-related language in edits after 2022, alongside recent declines in work-from-home and DEI terminology.
LLM-associated writing markers surge in profile text after the ChatGPT launch, "especially among less-educated groups and MBAs from lower-ranked programs."
methodology: Panel constructed from monthly vintages of Revelio Labs data covering 2020 to 2026, which allows the same worker-job record to be observed at multiple points in time and compared against its own earlier versions. Edits are identified by differencing successive vintages of the title and description fields for jobs whose end date has already passed. Editing behaviour is then related to observed employer changes and to the textual content of the revision, including AI-related terms and LLM-associated writing markers.
qualifiers: This paper contains no employment or wage estimate and maps to no prediction graph as a data point. Its relevance to this corpus is as a measurement caveat on sources built from public professional profiles, which on this site means the Revelio Labs series behind the early-career employment decline and twelve firm-side overlays. Note that two of the four authors are affiliated with Revelio Labs, so this is a vendor-documented limitation rather than an adversarial critique, which strengthens rather than weakens its standing. The paper establishes that bias exists and that it correlates with transitions and vocabulary, but it does not quantify the magnitude of the resulting error in any specific published employment estimate, so it cannot be used to adjust or discount any plotted value. The post-2022 rise in AI-related language in retroactive edits is the finding with the most direct bearing on this site: it implies that exposure or adoption measures derived from profile text partly capture workers relabelling past work in current vocabulary rather than the work itself changing.
